# Laying the Foundation for Economic Success, Brick by Brick

 July 8, 2011 at 6:12 PM ET by Ari Matusiak 

[Twitter](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=http%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick&text=Laying%20the%20Foundation%20for%20Economic%20Suc... "Twitter")[Facebook](http://facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick "Facebook")[Email](mailto:?to=&subject=&body=For%20years%2C%20Frank%20Cordie%20led%20a%20complex%20financing%20process%20to%20bring%20brick%20manufacturing%20back%20to%20Mexico%2C%20MO.%20His%20efforts%20have%20paid%20off%2C%20as%20Mid%20America%20Brick%2C%20the%20only%20brick%20manufacturer%20in%20central%20Missouri%2C%20has%20united%20community%20members%20and%20helped%20to%20revitalize%20the%20region%27s%20economy.%20%20%0Ahttp%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick "Email")

Summary:

For years, Frank Cordie led a complex financing process to bring brick manufacturing back to Mexico, MO. His efforts have paid off, as Mid America Brick, the only brick manufacturer in central Missouri, has united community members and helped to revitalize the region's economy. 

Frank Cordie grew up across the river from St. Louis, MO in Belleville, IL. After college, he took his first job at a refractory plant in Mexico, MO – the Fire Brick Capital of the World, and home to a leading refractory manufacturing company, A.P. Green Refractories. Frank spent the next 25 years working in the brick-manufacturing industry, managing several plants for multiple companies. Frank eventually returned to Mexico, MO as the Vice President of Manufacturing for A.P. Green. By the late 1990s, A.P. Green had been purchased by another company, and the refractory industry in the U.S. had consolidated to just a few manufacturers. Frank’s position meant he was responsible for, among other things, consolidating production and closing plants where necessary. The A.P. Green factory, a cornerstone of the Mexico community, was shuttered in 2002.

![Image 3: Mid America Brick Factory](https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/default/files/image/image_file/reading_machine_at_mid_america_brick.jpg)
Mid America Brick CEO Frank Cordie at the company's plant in Mexico, MO, July 6, 2011. (Photo by Employees of Mid America Brick)

In December 2006, Frank began a process to bring brick manufacturing back to Mexico, MO. His goal was to purchase and re-purpose the former A.P. Green plant to produce face brick used in residential and commercial construction. Engaging in what would be eventually described as “one of the most complicated financing projects in the United States” by partner Advantage Capital, the intricacies of the deal took almost four years to complete. Frank leveraged local, State, and Federal New Market Tax Credits, loans and loan guarantee programs – including a [Rural Business and Industry Loan Guarantee](http://www.rurdev.usda.gov/rbs/busp/b&i_gar.htm) from the USDA. An initial investment of $500,000 from an LLC formed by local businessmen – described by Frank as “the snowball at the top of the mountain” – eventually became a total startup investment of almost $22 million.

In addition to Advantage Capital, supporters in the venture included companies from Buffalo, NY, St. Louis, MO, and Knoxville, TN. A bipartisan group of city, state, and federal elected officials and legislators worked together to make the project a reality.

On June 25, 2010, [Mid America Brick](http://www.midamericabrick.com/) was unveiled with 400 community members in attendance 100 years after the founding of A.P. Green at the same location. The community has rallied around the project. Local accountants and lawyers provided services free of charge during the financing process, telling Frank they knew he’d reimburse them when the venture succeeded. A retired businessman and initial investor personally mowed the lawn, cleaned the parking lot, and provided a new flagpole for the facility in advance of the unveiling. Frank’s wife Judy worked to revive the Mexico community Christmas Tree lighting – a long standing tradition of the A.P. Green Company – last December. Retired A.P. Green employees volunteered time, expertise, and materials so Mid America Brick could hold an event for which they didn’t plan a budget. At the tree lighting, Judy and Frank collected donations for The Help Center, a local food pantry and clothing supplier for those in need.

Mid America Brick extruded its first brick on April 13, 2011. The company is now the only brick manufacturer in central Missouri. They have 42 full-time employees, and hope to expand to 75 employees by the end of next year, by which time they expect to produce over 60 million bricks annually. They have also supported related areas of labor, contracting out clay mining in the surrounding area, hauling and trucking 10-20 loads of clay and brick per day, and bringing in contractors for large maintenance projects. During the retrofitting of the facility, 50-75 workers assisted on construction, helping the hotel and restaurant industries in Mexico, MO. The company has also been recognized by the State of Missouri for its efforts employing veterans.

Mid America Brick is helping to lead a revitalization of Mexico, MO. Mid America Brick provides an independent, local source of bricks for residential and commercial construction in Missouri and surrounding states. The company’s goal is “to be the preferred brick supplier for all customers, by providing quality products and superior service.”

_Ari Matusiak is Executive Director of the White House Business Council_

# Laying the Foundation for Economic Success, Brick by Brick

 July 8, 2011 at 6:12 PM ET by Ari Matusiak 

[Twitter](http://twitter.com/intent/tweet?url=http%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick&text=Laying%20the%20Foundation%20for%20Economic%20Suc... "Twitter")[Facebook](http://facebook.com/sharer.php?u=http%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick "Facebook")[Email](mailto:?to=&subject=&body=For%20years%2C%20Frank%20Cordie%20led%20a%20complex%20financing%20process%20to%20bring%20brick%20manufacturing%20back%20to%20Mexico%2C%20MO.%20His%20efforts%20have%20paid%20off%2C%20as%20Mid%20America%20Brick%2C%20the%20only%20brick%20manufacturer%20in%20central%20Missouri%2C%20has%20united%20community%20members%20and%20helped%20to%20revitalize%20the%20region%27s%20economy.%20%20%0Ahttp%3A%2F%2Fobamawhitehouse.archives.gov%2Fblog%2F2011%2F07%2F08%2Flaying-foundation-economic-success-brick-brick "Email")

Summary:

For years, Frank Cordie led a complex financing process to bring brick manufacturing back to Mexico, MO. His efforts have paid off, as Mid America Brick, the only brick manufacturer in central Missouri, has united community members and helped to revitalize the region's economy. 

Frank Cordie grew up across the river from St. Louis, MO in Belleville, IL. After college, he took his first job at a refractory plant in Mexico, MO – the Fire Brick Capital of the World, and home to a leading refractory manufacturing company, A.P. Green Refractories. Frank spent the next 25 years working in the brick-manufacturing industry, managing several plants for multiple companies. Frank eventually returned to Mexico, MO as the Vice President of Manufacturing for A.P. Green. By the late 1990s, A.P. Green had been purchased by another company, and the refractory industry in the U.S. had consolidated to just a few manufacturers. Frank’s position meant he was responsible for, among other things, consolidating production and closing plants where necessary. The A.P. Green factory, a cornerstone of the Mexico community, was shuttered in 2002.

![Image 3: Mid America Brick Factory](https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/sites/default/files/image/image_file/reading_machine_at_mid_america_brick.jpg)
Mid America Brick CEO Frank Cordie at the company's plant in Mexico, MO, July 6, 2011. (Photo by Employees of Mid America Brick)

In December 2006, Frank began a process to bring brick manufacturing back to Mexico, MO. His goal was to purchase and re-purpose the former A.P. Green plant to produce face brick used in residential and commercial construction. Engaging in what would be eventually described as “one of the most complicated financing projects in the United States” by partner Advantage Capital, the intricacies of the deal took almost four years to complete. Frank leveraged local, State, and Federal New Market Tax Credits, loans and loan guarantee programs – including a [Rural Business and Industry Loan Guarantee](http://www.rurdev.usda.gov/rbs/busp/b&i_gar.htm) from the USDA. An initial investment of $500,000 from an LLC formed by local businessmen – described by Frank as “the snowball at the top of the mountain” – eventually became a total startup investment of almost $22 million.

In addition to Advantage Capital, supporters in the venture included companies from Buffalo, NY, St. Louis, MO, and Knoxville, TN. A bipartisan group of city, state, and federal elected officials and legislators worked together to make the project a reality.

On June 25, 2010, [Mid America Brick](http://www.midamericabrick.com/) was unveiled with 400 community members in attendance 100 years after the founding of A.P. Green at the same location. The community has rallied around the project. Local accountants and lawyers provided services free of charge during the financing process, telling Frank they knew he’d reimburse them when the venture succeeded. A retired businessman and initial investor personally mowed the lawn, cleaned the parking lot, and provided a new flagpole for the facility in advance of the unveiling. Frank’s wife Judy worked to revive the Mexico community Christmas Tree lighting – a long standing tradition of the A.P. Green Company – last December. Retired A.P. Green employees volunteered time, expertise, and materials so Mid America Brick could hold an event for which they didn’t plan a budget. At the tree lighting, Judy and Frank collected donations for The Help Center, a local food pantry and clothing supplier for those in need.

Mid America Brick extruded its first brick on April 13, 2011. The company is now the only brick manufacturer in central Missouri. They have 42 full-time employees, and hope to expand to 75 employees by the end of next year, by which time they expect to produce over 60 million bricks annually. They have also supported related areas of labor, contracting out clay mining in the surrounding area, hauling and trucking 10-20 loads of clay and brick per day, and bringing in contractors for large maintenance projects. During the retrofitting of the facility, 50-75 workers assisted on construction, helping the hotel and restaurant industries in Mexico, MO. The company has also been recognized by the State of Missouri for its efforts employing veterans.

Mid America Brick is helping to lead a revitalization of Mexico, MO. Mid America Brick provides an independent, local source of bricks for residential and commercial construction in Missouri and surrounding states. The company’s goal is “to be the preferred brick supplier for all customers, by providing quality products and superior service.”

_Ari Matusiak is Executive Director of the White House Business Council_

AP Green produced bricks in Mexico from 1910 to 2002. The factory has been sitting silent for the last eight years. Frank Cordie began the efforts to restart the factory three years ago.

Cordie and his supporters secured half of the renovation's $21.9 million through grants, tax credits, and loans.

"We're showing the rest of the country that rural America is alive and well," said Cordie, Mid America Brick's president and CEO.

Anna Marie Alderson's late husband Joe worked for AP Green for 42 years. She says he would be thrilled to know that the plant will start production again at the beginning of 2011. She credits the mutual loyalty between her husband and AP Green for their lifestyle.

"Everything we own, everything we had came from this acreage of the AP Green plant," said Alderson.

Cordie and Alderson both say the community played a large part in bringing back the brick factory.

"The town has banded together to bring it into existence," said Alderson. "It's just wonderful."

AP Green's bricks were shipped all over the United States. Alderson's husband was a lift truck operator and she says he knew where all the bricks he loaded went. He felt especially proud to be a part of the factory when the bricks went to aid the World War II efforts.

Mid America Brick plans on starting on a smaller scale. It will hire about 80 people by the end of the year and produce face bricks for residential and commercial construction. Several politicans who helped get financial support were at the ceremony.

"It'll offer lower freight costs, shorter freight routes to other midwest destinations, which should keep construction costs down for a struggling home building industry," said Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri. "But it will also provide high quality products that will keep buyers coming back."

"I want to see it grow and hire many men who have lost their jobs in this area," said Alderson.

AP Green produced bricks in Mexico from 1910 to 2002. The factory has been sitting silent for the last eight years. Frank Cordie began the efforts to restart the factory three years ago.

Cordie and his supporters secured half of the renovation's $21.9 million through grants, tax credits, and loans.

"We're showing the rest of the country that rural America is alive and well," said Cordie, Mid America Brick's president and CEO.

Anna Marie Alderson's late husband Joe worked for AP Green for 42 years. She says he would be thrilled to know that the plant will start production again at the beginning of 2011. She credits the mutual loyalty between her husband and AP Green for their lifestyle.

"Everything we own, everything we had came from this acreage of the AP Green plant," said Alderson.

Cordie and Alderson both say the community played a large part in bringing back the brick factory.

"The town has banded together to bring it into existence," said Alderson. "It's just wonderful."

AP Green's bricks were shipped all over the United States. Alderson's husband was a lift truck operator and she says he knew where all the bricks he loaded went. He felt especially proud to be a part of the factory when the bricks went to aid the World War II efforts.

Mid America Brick plans on starting on a smaller scale. It will hire about 80 people by the end of the year and produce face bricks for residential and commercial construction. Several politicans who helped get financial support were at the ceremony.

"It'll offer lower freight costs, shorter freight routes to other midwest destinations, which should keep construction costs down for a struggling home building industry," said Sen. Kit Bond, R-Missouri. "But it will also provide high quality products that will keep buyers coming back."

"I want to see it grow and hire many men who have lost their jobs in this area," said Alderson.

# ‘Firebrick Capital’ looks to face brick for jobs

Justin Willett

Updated June 5, 2010, 7:00 a.m. CT

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=614332612831567&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F&text=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs&via=columbiatribune)[](mailto:?subject=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs%20-%20from%20Columbia%20Daily%20Tribune&body=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs%0A%0AMexico%2C%20Mo.%2C%20once%20again%20will%20be%20the%20home%20to%20a%20brick-making%20facility%2C%20but%20this%20time%20it%20will%20produce%20bricks%20for%20the%20homebuilding%20market%20and%20not%20to%20line%20furnaces.%20%0A%20Once%20known%20as%20the%20%E2%80%9CFirebrick%20Capital%20%E2%80%A6%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20columbiatribune.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F)

Mexico, Mo., once again will be the home to a brick-making facility, but this time it will produce bricks for the homebuilding market and not to line furnaces.

Once known as the “Firebrick Capital of the World” for its abundance of manufacturers of bricks used to line industrial furnaces, Mexico saw its economic fortunes dwindle as the brick facilities closed one by one.

[End of an era for Cleek’s](http://archive.columbiatribune.com/2008/dec/20081205busi009.asp)[Top 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma Maters](http://www.businessweek.com/magazine/content/10_21/b4179020050124.htm)[Kampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant](http://www.facebook.com/pages/Columbia-MO/Kampai-Alley/110150395684079)Football is back: [Stream every big game, rivalry matchup and can't-miss moment all season long](https://www.usatoday.com/story/shopping/sports/streaming/2026/09/08/how-to-watch-every-nfl-game-this-season/91643587007/?utm_source=networkpromo&utm_medium=spikelink&utm_campaign=nfl_kickoff_2026)[Midway USA](http://midwayusa.com/)
The A.P. Green firebrick plant, which had been in operation since 1910, closed in 2001. At its height during World War II, the plant employed nearly 4,000 workers. At the end it had 118 on its payroll. The following year, 2002, Mexico’s last brick factory closed, taking with it 200 jobs.

This week, on the 100th anniversary of the opening of the A.P. Green factory, Mid America Brick & Structural Clay Products LLC closed on the purchase of 100 acres and the buildings on the former A.P. Green site.

The cost of the purchase and for recommissioning the 500,000-square-foot former A.P. Green facility is $21.9 million.

Mexico became the so-called “Firebrick Capital of the World” because the region’s clay was so heat-resistant and conducive to making firebricks, which are used in industrial furnaces. Mexico icon A.P. Green, maternal grandfather of U.S. Sen. Kit Bond, wrote that he thought “the quality of Missouri clays, if properly exploited, would result in establishing Missouri as the leading fire brick business in the United States and later of the world.”

However, with the decline in the industries that use such furnaces — steel, cement and others — the demand has declined. Mid America Brick will manufacture so-called face brick, which is used for residential and commercial construction.

CEO Frank Cordie said in a statement that when fully operational, the company will create as many as 80 new jobs and produce more than 60 million bricks per year. Vice President David Adams said the company hopes to begin producing bricks by next spring.

Adams said they’re confident in the market because homebuilding is picking up and face brick inventories are at all-time lows. He said the closest face brick plant is in Jackson in southeast Missouri.

“It’s great news for us,” Adams said of the building turnaround, “in addition to brick inventories are at the lowest level they’ve been in some time. We look forward to capitalizing on that.”

The deal for the A.P. Green property, which has been in the works for four years, included local, state and federal grants and loans.

St. Louis-based Advantage Capital Partners provided $9.75 million for the project.

NO NEEEED FOR A BUILDING

The former Cleek’s store at Worley Street and West Boulevard has been demolished, and property owner and local rent-to-own king “Tiger” John Cleek said he’s looking at a couple of different options for the property.

Cleek estimates the building is about 60 years old. He moved out his business about 18 months ago when he joined Aaron Rents Inc. and set up shop at the Aaron’s store on Business Loop 70 West.

The building had been remodeled in 2004, but Cleek says it “just needed more work done to it than was reasonable to do to it.”

Cleek said the building was home to Bob’s Market when he was a child. and his father bought it in 1971. Cleek moved in in August 1973.

SUNDAY NEWS

KMIZ-TV is introducing a 30-minute community affairs show called “ABC 17 News This Week.” The first episode is scheduled for 11 a.m. tomorrow. The show will be hosted by anchor Ryan Tate and feature in-depth exploration of community issues, said ABC 17 News Director Curtis Varns. Tomorrow’s broadcast will be a look at the state budget.

Varns said he has been at the station for more than 15 years and during that time they’ve added about nine hours of news to each broadcast week, but this is the first regularly scheduled 30-minute newsmagazine the station has done.

“Money has been so tight on the federal, state and local levels the past few years that people are looking for accountability in their elected officials more than ever,” Varns said. “We try to take a critical look at the issues every time we cover state and local government in our nightly news. We should be able to build on that effort in this format.”

**The University of Missouri** made an appearance on BusinessWeek.com’s Top 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma Maters list. MU tied with Harvard, the University of Texas and the University of Wisconsin with 11 CEOs. David Novak of Yum! Brands was highlighted on the list for MU. … Internet shooting retailer **Midway USA** has branched out into archery gear. The company that bills itself as offering “Just About Everything for Shooting, Reloading, Gunsmithing and Hunting” has now begun offering arrows and arrow shafts; broadheads and points; archery sights; shooting releases; quivers; archery targets; bow cases; and bow tuning products. … **Kampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant,** 907 Alley A, is now open. The restaurant, owned by Art Wuttisak, Tony Sudsai and Sam Tuankrua, is near Ninth Street, just south of Broadway.

# ‘Firebrick Capital’ looks to face brick for jobs

Justin Willett

Updated June 5, 2010, 7:00 a.m. CT

[](https://www.facebook.com/dialog/share?display=popup&app_id=614332612831567&href=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F)[](https://x.com/intent/post?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F&text=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs&via=columbiatribune)[](mailto:?subject=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs%20-%20from%20Columbia%20Daily%20Tribune&body=%E2%80%98Firebrick%20Capital%E2%80%99%20looks%20to%20face%20brick%20for%20jobs%0A%0AMexico%2C%20Mo.%2C%20once%20again%20will%20be%20the%20home%20to%20a%20brick-making%20facility%2C%20but%20this%20time%20it%20will%20produce%20bricks%20for%20the%20homebuilding%20market%20and%20not%20to%20line%20furnaces.%20%0A%20Once%20known%20as%20the%20%E2%80%9CFirebrick%20Capital%20%E2%80%A6%0A%0ACheck%20out%20this%20story%20on%20columbiatribune.com%3A%20https%3A%2F%2Fwww.columbiatribune.com%2Fstory%2Fbusiness%2F2010%2F06%2F05%2Ffirebrick-capital-looks-to%2F21491021007%2F)

Mexico, Mo., once again will be the home to a brick-making facility, but this time it will produce bricks for the homebuilding market and not to line furnaces.

Once known as the “Firebrick Capital of the World” for its abundance of manufacturers of bricks used to line industrial furnaces, Mexico saw its economic fortunes dwindle as the brick facilities closed one by one.

[End of an era for Cleek’s](http://archive.columbiatribune.com/2008/dec/20081205busi009.asp)[Top 10 CEO Undergraduate Alma Maters](http://www.businessweek.com/magazine/content/10_21/b4179020050124.htm)[Kampai Sushi Bar & Restaurant](http://www.facebook.com/pages/Columbia-MO/Kampai-Alley/110150395684079)Football is back: [Stream every big game, rivalry matchup and can't-miss moment all season long](https://www.usatoday.com/story/shopping/sports/streaming/2026/09/08/how-to-watch-every-nfl-game-this-season/91643587007/?utm_source=networkpromo&utm_medium=spikelink&utm_campaign=nfl_kickoff_2026)[Midway USA](http://midwayusa.com/)
The A.P. Green firebrick plant, which had been in operation since 1910, closed in 2001. At its height during World War II, the plant employed nearly 4,000 workers. At the end it had 118 on its payroll. The following year, 2002, Mexico’s last brick factory closed, taking with it 200 jobs.

This week, on the 100th anniversary of the opening of the A.P. Green factory, Mid America Brick & Structural Clay Products LLC closed on the purchase of 100 acres and the buildings on the former A.P. Green site.

The cost of the purchase and for recommissioning the 500,000-square-foot former A.P. Green facility is $21.9 million.

Mexico became the so-called “Firebrick Capital of the World” because the region’s clay was so heat-resistant and conducive to making firebricks, which are used in industrial furnaces. Mexico icon A.P. Green, maternal grandfather of U.S. Sen. Kit Bond, wrote that he thought “the quality of Missouri clays, if properly exploited, would result in establishing Missouri as the leading fire brick business in the United States and later of the world.”

However, with the decline in the industries that use such furnaces — steel, cement and others — the demand has declined. Mid America Brick will manufacture so-called face brick, which is used for residential and commercial construction.

CEO Frank Cordie said in a statement that when fully operational, the company will create as many as 80 new jobs and produce more than 60 million bricks per year. Vice President David Adams said the company hopes to begin producing bricks by next spring.

Adams said they’re confident in the market because homebuilding is picking up and face brick inventories are at all-time lows. He said the closest face brick plant is in Jackson in southeast Missouri.

“It’s great news for us,” Adams said of the building turnaround, “in addition to brick inventories are at the lowest level they’ve been in some time. We look forward to capitalizing on that.”

The deal for the A.P. Green property, which has been in the works for four years, included local, state and federal grants and loans.

St. Louis-based Advantage Capital Partners provided $9.75 million for the project.

NO NEEEED FOR A BUILDING

The former Cleek’s store at Worley Street and West Boulevard has been demolished, and property owner and local rent-to-own king “Tiger” John Cleek said he’s looking at a couple of different options for the property.

Cleek estimates the building is about 60 years old. He moved out his business about 18 months ago when he joined Aaron Rents Inc. and set up shop at the Aaron’s store on Business Loop 70 West.

The building had been remodeled in 2004, but Cleek says it “just needed more work done to it than was reasonable to do to it.”

Cleek said the building was home to Bob’s Market when he was a child. and his father bought it in 1971. Cleek moved in in August 1973.

SUNDAY NEWS

KMIZ-TV is introducing a 30-minute community affairs show called “ABC 17 News This Week.” The first episode is scheduled for 11 a.m. tomorrow. The show will be hosted by anchor Ryan Tate and feature in-depth exploration of community issues, said ABC 17 News Director Curtis Varns. Tomorrow’s broadcast will be a look at the state budget.

Varns said he has been at the station for more than 15 years and during that time they’ve added about nine hours of news to each broadcast week, but this is the first regularly scheduled 30-minute newsmagazine the station has done.

“Money has been so tight on the federal, state and local levels the past few years that people are looking for accountability in their elected officials more than ever,” Varns said. “We try to take a critical look at the issues every time we cover state and local government in our nightly news. We should be able to build on that effort in this format.”

*   ## Buses & Transporation

Registration and bus route sign-up close August 11; bus routes will be compiled immediately following. Registrations received after August 11 may not receive bus placement until after school has started.

**[Register a rider here.](https://parents.busright.com/2rz1csysdg)Use BusRight to log in and register a student rider.**

Parents are encouraged to download the BusRight app to see your child’s route and be able to view when the bus is within five minutes of the bus stop.

If the home address is over 1 mile from the students school, they qualify for transportation. Any students who live under 1 mile from their school, does not qualify but can be put on a paid rider waitlist. There are a few exceptions for special circumstances. If you have any questions regarding this or are unsure of the distance, please give the Transportation office a call.

Paid Riders will be placed on a waitlist pending placement. You will be contacted by the transportation office for placement if there is available seating to accommodate paid riders. Pricing is as follows:

    *   One way (AM only or PM only): $20.00 per month
    *   Both ways (AM & PM): $40.00 Per month
    *   Discount offered for siblings

Due to driver shortages and route changes, please keep in mind that routes may be different than previous year. Driver, stop location, and bus number are subject to change.

Bus assignments/passes will be sent out via email. Please make sure your contact information is up-to-date and correct. Route information will also be viewable in the BusRight app. Route Information will be sent out no later than August 20, 2026.

**Questions?** The Transportation Department can be reached at the Central Office by calling 573-581-3773 or emailing ineeley@mexico.k12.mo.us.

*   ## Class Schedules & Teacher Assignments

Elementary teacher assignments and middle/high school schedules will be shared with registered students the week before school starts. Parents/guardians will receive a notification from the school district when the information is available. 
*   ## School Communications

Mexico Public Schools uses a variety of methods of communication to share school-related news, reminders, and important information with parents, guardians, and the community.

For parents/guardians with district students, it is important that you have a current email address and cell phone number in your Infinite Campus parent portal. Please check to make sure your contact information is up-to-date so you receive all school-related communication from the district, building principals, and your child’s teachers.

The primary method of communication for the district and schools is ParentSquare. The district and school buildings will send emails and text messages to parents/guardians about important reminders, time-sensitive updates, and any other urgent matters.
